summary: Non-variceal and variceal upper GI bleeds are managed differently in several important ways — variceal bleeding specifically needs three concurrent therapies (not sequential trial-and-error), a restrictive transfusion target that's easy to over-shoot out of habit, and balloon tamponade is a bridge, never a destination.
whyThisMatters: In known or suspected variceal hemorrhage, transfusing to a normal hemoglobin can actively worsen bleeding by raising portal pressure — the instinct to 'give more blood to a bleeding patient' is exactly backwards here, and it's one of the more counterintuitive, easy-to-get-wrong management points in emergency/critical care.
clinicalTakeaway: For suspected variceal hemorrhage in a cirrhotic patient: start octreotide AND prophylactic antibiotics immediately, and arrange endoscopy within 12 hours — all three, not just one. Transfuse to a restrictive target (Hgb ~7 g/dL, slightly higher with active hemodynamic instability) rather than chasing a normal number. If bleeding is refractory and endoscopy/TIPS isn't immediately available, balloon tamponade is a temporizing bridge only.

body.text: Initial resuscitation — restrictive transfusion, and why it matters more here

Restrictive transfusion (target hemoglobin ~7 g/dL, higher if actively unstable or with significant cardiac disease) is standard for upper GI bleeding generally, but the rationale is STRONGER in variceal bleeding specifically: over-transfusing raises intravascular volume and portal pressure, which can directly worsen ongoing variceal bleeding — this isn't just 'avoid unnecessary transfusion,' it's 'over-transfusion can actively make this specific bleed worse.' Resist the reflex to transfuse toward a normal hemoglobin in a hemodynamically stable variceal bleeder.
Suspected variceal hemorrhage — three concurrent therapies

items: Octreotide: bolus followed by continuous infusion, started as soon as variceal bleeding is suspected (known cirrhosis, stigmata of portal hypertension, or a bleed severe enough to warrant treating empirically pending endoscopy) — reduces splanchnic blood flow and portal pressure.

Prophylactic antibiotics: started at the same time, not held pending evidence of infection. This is a genuinely important, sometimes-overlooked point — antibiotic prophylaxis in cirrhotic patients with GI bleeding reduces MORTALITY, independent of whether an infection is clinically apparent at presentation, likely by preventing the bacterial translocation and subsequent infection/rebleeding cascade that complicates cirrhotic GI bleeds.

Endoscopy within 12 hours for both diagnosis and therapy (band ligation for esophageal varices; other techniques for gastric varices) — this is a hard target in the variceal-bleeding literature, not a loose guideline.

body.text: All three — octreotide, antibiotics, and timely endoscopy — should be started/arranged together in suspected variceal hemorrhage, not tried one at a time. Withholding antibiotics until 'proof' of infection, or delaying octreotide until endoscopy confirms varices, both give up real mortality benefit for no good reason.
Refractory bleeding — balloon tamponade is a bridge, not a destination

Balloon tamponade (e.g. a Sengstaken-Blakemore or Minnesota tube) can temporarily control bleeding by direct compression, for life-threatening variceal hemorrhage:
- refractory to the above
- uncontrolled by endoscopy
- or when endoscopy/interventional radiology isn't immediately available

This is explicitly temporizing — rebleeding is common once deflated, and prolonged inflation risks esophageal/gastric mucosal ischemia and perforation.

Use it as a bridge to definitive therapy (repeat endoscopy, or TIPS — transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt — for genuinely refractory bleeding), with a clear plan for what happens next, not as an endpoint.
Non-variceal upper GI bleed — where the approach diverges

items: High-dose PPI (e.g. an IV bolus followed by continuous infusion or high-dose intermittent dosing) rather than octreotide — the mechanism (reducing acid to stabilize a clot over an ulcer) is different from the portal-pressure-lowering goal of octreotide, and octreotide has no established role here.

No mandatory antibiotic-prophylaxis analog exists for non-variceal bleeding the way it does for variceal bleeding in cirrhotics — the mortality-benefit data specifically concerns the cirrhotic/variceal population.

Endoscopy timing is generally within 24 hours (versus the tighter 12-hour variceal target), risk-stratified by clinical severity (existing risk scores like Glasgow-Blatchford help triage who needs it soonest).

The restrictive-transfusion-worsens-variceal-bleeding mechanism is stated explicitly since it's the single most counterintuitive, most likely-to-be-gotten-wrong point in this content.
